analysis.one_liner: Requires online video, video calls, and devices to be accessible to deaf and blind users.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final weeks of the 117th Congress, the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its communications subcommittee, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill updates the 2010 disability accessibility law for the internet era. It would require closed captioning and audio description on online video, not just TV; accessible video conferencing with built-in captions; easier-to-use caption and audio-description controls on remotes and devices; better relay services so deaf and DeafBlind callers can reach 911 directly in American Sign Language; and it doubles federal funding for distributing specialized equipment to DeafBlind individuals.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind, low-vision, or DeafBlind, who would gain guaranteed access to captions, audio description, American Sign Language interpretation, accessible video calling, and direct ASL access to 911.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to extend closed captioning rules to video programming delivered over the internet, including on-demand and streamed programming, on a phased schedule the bill allows to run up to six years after a report to the Commission [S3].

Requires audio description on both televised and online video programming, with labeling, a dedicated audio channel, and quality standards, plus uniform standards for American Sign Language interpretation displayed on screen [S3].

Requires video conferencing services to fall under the accessibility rules for advanced communications, with built-in closed captioning, compatibility with screen readers, braille displays, and third-party interpreting services, and lets users control captions and interpreters independent of the meeting host [S3].

Requires devices and remotes to have dedicated, tactilely identifiable buttons for captions and audio description, settings that persist across apps and restarts, and hardware compatible with braille displays, sip-and-puff devices, and hearing aids [S3].

Expands telecommunications relay services to include communication facilitators for DeafBlind callers and direct video calling, and requires full, equal, direct access to 911 for ASL users with location transmitted as fast as a voice call [S3].
Doubles the National DeafBlind Equipment Distribution Program's funding from $10 million to $20 million, adjusted annually for inflation [S3].
Strengthens enforcement by making FCC forfeiture penalties expressly available for accessibility violations, and requires regular reports to Congress on complaints and their resolution [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Video streaming platforms, video conferencing providers, and consumer electronics makers would bear captioning, audio description, and equipment compliance costs; video conferencing providers would also newly pay into the relay services fund that pays for deaf callers' services.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on online video platforms and on user-generated video creators earning more than $1 million annually from user-generated content, which the bill brings within captioning obligations [S3].
Video conferencing providers must newly contribute to the telecommunications relay services fund and build in captioning, adding direct costs for widely used business and consumer tools [S3].
Device requirements — dedicated buttons, persistent settings, compatibility hardware — could add design and manufacturing costs across remotes, TVs, and streaming devices [S3].
Many benefits are slow: captioning rules for online video can phase in up to six years after the advisory committee's report, so deaf and blind viewers would wait years for full access [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for roughly tens of millions of deaf, hard-of-hearing, blind, and DeafBlind Americans — access to news, entertainment, work meetings, and 911 — are substantial and the bill is carefully designed, with economic-burden exemptions, phased deadlines, and industry representation on its advisory committees. The costs are real but spread across large technology and media companies, and much of it is work the industry already performs on major platforms voluntarily. The main honest criticism is the long phase-in, which delays the very access the bill promises.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the last weeks of the session, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its communications subcommittee, and no committee or floor action ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Anna Eshoo introduced the bill on November 17, 2022, with four Democratic cosponsors, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day referred it to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology [S5].
No markup, vote, or further action followed; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

The bill would have extended closed captioning and audio description requirements from television to internet-delivered video and expanded relay and emergency access for deaf and DeafBlind callers [S2][S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Streaming platforms, video conferencing providers, and device manufacturers avoided new captioning, audio description, and equipment mandates, while deaf and blind Americans continued without guaranteed online access.

for.name: Rep. Anna Eshoo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the House.

for.name: Reps. Mary Gay Scanlon, Eleanor Holmes Norton, Katie Porter, and Mike Levin
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral; never acted on the bill
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out or scheduled a markup before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Support was exclusively Democratic — the sponsor and all four cosponsors — but the bill died in committee without a recorded vote, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Video streaming and online video platforms
industries.note: The bill would require closed captioning and audio description on internet-delivered video, including user-generated video from creators earning over $1 million, with quality standards and phased deadlines. Their compliance costs are the price of deaf and blind viewers getting equal access to the same programming.

The bill would subject video conferencing services and equipment to accessibility rules, require built-in closed captioning and compatibility with assistive technology, and make providers pay into the telecommunications relay services fund for the first time. Costs to them fund the relay services their deaf users depend on.

Remotes and devices would need dedicated, tactile caption and audio-description buttons, persistent settings, and compatibility with braille displays and other assistive hardware. Compliance is device-level engineering work whose benefit goes to users with disabilities.

industries.industry: Captioning, audio description, and relay service providers
industries.note: Extending captioning, audio description, direct video calling, and communication facilitators to online video and video calls creates demand for the vendors that produce these services.
